title: DOT Advisory Committee on Human Trafficking
content: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION Office of the Secretary of Transportation [Docket No.: DOT-OST-2026-3598] DOT Advisory Committee on Human Trafficking AGENCY: Office of the Secretary of Transportation (OST), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT). ACTION: Notice of public meetings. SUMMARY: The Office of the Secretary of Transportation (OST) announces the DOT Advisory Committee on Human Trafficking's public meetings in 2026 and 2027. This notice announces the dates, times, and locations of the virtual meetings, which will be open to the public. The purpose of the ACHT is to advise the Secretary of Transportation on countering human trafficking in the transportation sector. DATES: The meetings will be held as follows: • Meeting 1 : November 4, 2026, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. EST • Meeting 2: December 10, 2026, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. EST • Meeting 3: January 28, 2027, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. EST • Meeting 4: May 20, 2027, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. EDT • Meeting 5: June 17, 2027, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. EDT • Meeting 6: July 8, 2027, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. EDT The exact start and end times are subject to change; please monitor https://www.transportation.gov/stop-human-trafficking/acht for the latest information. ADDRESSES: The ACHT will meet virtually. The public may join the meetings virtually, with information available at https://www.transportation.gov/stop-human-trafficking/acht. FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: The ACHT's Designated Federal Officer, Maha Alkhateeb, Senior Counter-Trafficking Advisor, Office of International Transportation and Trade, Office of the Secretary, at trafficking@dot.gov or (202) 366-4398. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Background The ACHT makes triennial recommendations to the Secretary of Transportation on countering human trafficking in the transportation sector. The ACHT was originally established as a statutory committee on October 3, 2018, pursuant to section 5(a) of the 2018 Combating Human Trafficking in Commercial Vehicles Act (Pub. L. 115-99). The ACHT was reestablished as a continuing committee on July 29, 2022, in accordance with section 23020 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (Pub. L. 117-58), which requires the Secretary of Transportation, acting through the ACHT and in coordination with the Attorney General, to submit a triennial counter-trafficking report with recommendations for countering human trafficking, an assessment of best practices by transportation stakeholders, and human trafficking violations involving commercial motor vehicles. Agenda At the meetings, the proposed agendas will cover the Call to Order, Administrative and Committee Business, Panels and Briefings, and Committee Deliberations. The agendas are subject to change. Public Participation The meetings will be open to the public through a virtual meeting. Registration for the meetings can be found here: https://www.transportation.gov/stop-human-trafficking/acht. Members of the public may submit comments to the Committee in advance, as well as any requests for an electronic meeting accommodation consistent with the relevant sections of the Rehabilitation Act, as amended, 29 U.S.C. 794, by contacting the individual listed in the For Further Information Contact section of this notice no later than 7 days prior to each meeting. All advance submissions will be reviewed by the Designated Federal Officer. If approved, advance submissions shall be circulated to the Committee members for review prior to the meeting. All advance submissions will become part of the official record of the meeting. Issued in Washington, DC, on October 13, 2026. Daniel J. Edwards, Assistant Secretary for Aviation and International Affairs. [FR Doc. 2026-21273 Filed 10-16-26; 8:45 am] BILLING CODE 4910-9X-P

title: Approval and Promulgation of Implementation Plans-Pinal County (Part); West Pinal, AZ PM10 Nonattainment Area; Moderate Area, Serious Area, and Section 189(d) Plan for Attainment of the 24-Hour PM10 Standard
content: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY 40 CFR Part 52 [EPA-R09-OAR-2026-5119; FRL-13482-01-R9] Approval and Promulgation of Implementation Plans—Pinal County (Part); West Pinal, AZ PM 10 Nonattainment Area; Moderate Area, Serious Area, and Section 189(d) Plan for Attainment of the 24-Hour PM 10 Standard AGENCY: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). ACTION: Proposed rule. SUMMARY: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to approve a state implementation plan (SIP) revision submitted by the State of Arizona to meet Clean Air Act (CAA or “Act”) requirements applicable to the Pinal County (Part); West Pinal PM 10 nonattainment area (“West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area”). The EPA is proposing to find that the submitted SIP revision meets all applicable “Moderate” area, “Serious” area, and CAA section 189(d) requirements for the PM 10 national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS). Additionally, the EPA is proposing to approve the PM 10 motor vehicle emissions budgets included with the SIP revision for transportation conformity purposes. The EPA is also starting the adequacy process for these budgets. Our proposed approval of the SIP revision would establish an attainment date of December 31, 2026, for the area. DATES: Comments must be received on or before November 18, 2026. ADDRESSES: Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-R09-OAR-2026-5119 at https://www.regulations.gov. For comments submitted at Regulations.gov , follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Once submitted, comments cannot be edited or removed from Regulations.gov . The EPA may publish any comment received to its public docket. Do not submit electronically any information you consider to be Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. Multimedia submissions (audio, video, etc.) must be accompanied by a written comment. The written comment is considered the official comment and should include discussion of all points you wish to make. The EPA will generally not consider comments or comment contents located outside of the primary submission ( i.e., on the web, cloud, or other file sharing system). For additional submission methods, please contact the person identified in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section. For the full EPA public comment policy, information about CBI or multimedia submissions, and general guidance on making effective comments, please visit https://www.epa.gov/dockets/commenting-epa-dockets. If you need assistance in a language other than English or if you are a person with a disability who needs a reasonable accommodation at no cost to you, please contact the person identified in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section. FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Jennifer Williams, EPA Region IX, 75 Hawthorne St., San Francisco, CA 94105. By telephone: (213) 244-1824, or by email at williams.jennifer@epa.gov. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Throughout this proposed rule, the use of “we,” “us,” or “our” is intended to refer to the EPA. We use multiple abbreviations and terms in this proposed rule. While this list may not be exhaustive, for ease of reading and for reference purposes, the EPA defines the following terms and acronyms here: ADEQ Arizona Department of Environmental Quality BACM Best Available Control Measures BACT Best Available Control Technology CAA Clean Air Act CBI Confidential Business Information EI Emissions Inventory EPA U.S. Environmental Protection Agency FHWA Federal Highway Administration FTA Federal Transit Administration MAG Maricopa Association of Governments µg/m 3 Micrograms per Cubic Meter MPO Metropolitan Planning Organization NAAQS National Ambient Air Quality Standards NEI National Emission Inventory NH 3 Ammonia NO X Oxides of Nitrogen PCAQCD Pinal County Air Quality Control District PM Particulate Matter PM 10 Particulate Matter with a Diameter of Ten Microns or Less RACM Reasonably Available Control Measures RFP Reasonable Further Progress SIP State Implementation Plan SO 2 Sulfur Dioxide TSD Technical Support Document VOC Volatile Organic Compounds VMT Vehicle Miles Traveled West Pinal County Pinal County (Part); West Pinal Table of Contents I. Executive Summary A. What proposed action is the EPA taking? B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? II. PM 10 Air Quality Planning in the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area III. Overview of Applicable CAA Requirements A. Emissions Inventories B. PM 10 Precursors C. Best Available Control Measures and Reasonably Available Control Measures Demonstration D. CAA Section 189(d) Attainment Demonstration and Five Percent Requirement E. Reasonable Further Progress and Quantitative Milestones F. Contingency Measures G. Transportation Conformity and Motor Vehicle Emissions Budgets H. Adequate Authority IV. Evaluation of the 2023 Five Percent Plan's Compliance With CAA Requirements A. Emissions Inventories B. PM 10 Precursors C. Best Available Control Measures and Reasonably Available Control Measures Demonstration D. CAA Section 189(d) Attainment Demonstration and Five Percent Requirement E. Reasonable Further Progress and Quantitative Milestones F. Contingency Measures G. Transportation Conformity and Motor Vehicle Emissions Budgets H. Adequate Legal Authority V. Summary of Proposed Actions VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews I. Executive Summary A. What proposed action is the EPA taking? The EPA is proposing to approve a SIP revision submitted by the State of Arizona to meet all Moderate area, Serious area, and CAA section 189(d) requirements applicable to the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area for the PM 10 NAAQS. The EPA is also proposing to approve the PM 10 motor vehicle emissions budgets included with the SIP revision for transportation conformity purposes and is starting the adequacy process for these budgets. B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? CAA sections 188 and 189 contain specific planning and control requirements relevant to the PM 10 NAAQS while CAA sections 110 and 172 contain general planning and control requirements for all nonattainment plans. The EPA is proposing approval of the baseline and attainment year emission inventory requirements of CAA section 172(c)(3), the BACM demonstration requirements of CAA section 189(b)(1)(B), the RACM demonstration requirements of CAA sections 189(a)(1)(C) and 172(c)(1), the attainment demonstration requirements of CAA sections 189(d) and 179(d)(3), the five percent demonstration requirements of CAA section 189(d), the reasonable further progress and quantitative milestone demonstration requirements of CAA sections 172(c)(2) and 189(c), the contingency measures requirements of CAA section 172(c)(9), and the motor vehicle emissions budgets as meeting the criteria for budgets in CAA section 176(c) and 40 CFR 93.118(e). The EPA is also starting the adequacy process for these budgets under 40 CFR 93.188(f). II. PM 10 Air Quality Planning in the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area The NAAQS are standards for certain ambient air pollutants set by the EPA to protect public health and welfare. Particulate matter with a diameter of ten microns or less (PM 10 ) is among the ambient air pollutants for which the EPA has established health-based standards. PM 10 causes adverse health effects by penetrating deep in the lungs, aggravating the cardiopulmonary system. Children, the elderly, and people with asthma and heart conditions are the most vulnerable. On July 1, 1987, the EPA revised the health-based NAAQS for particulate matter, establishing two PM 10 standards, an annual standard and a 24-hour standard. 1 Effective December 18, 2006, the EPA revoked the annual PM 10 standard but retained the 24-hour PM 10 standard. 2 The 24-hour PM 10 standard of 150 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m 3 ) is attained when the expected number of days with a 24-hour average concentration above 150 µg/m 3 per calendar year averaged over a three-year period, as determined in accordance with appendix K to 40 CFR part 50, is equal to or less than one. 3 1 52 FR 24672 (July 1, 1987). 2 71 FR 61144 (Oct. 17, 2006). 3 40 CFR 50.6 and 40 CFR part 50, appendix K. On May 31, 2012, the EPA designated a portion of State lands in Pinal County, Arizona (“West Pinal County”) as nonattainment for the 1987 PM 10 NAAQS based on 2006-2008 data. 4 West Pinal County is located in central Arizona, southeast of the Phoenix metropolitan area and northwest of the city of Tucson. Pinal County covers 5,365 square miles and has two distinct western and eastern regions with different characteristics relevant to pollution formation. The West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area is located within the western region, characterized by low desert valleys and an arid climate. The eastern region is mountainous, with elevations up to 6,441 feet. The West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area encompasses all land geographically located within Pinal County west of the north-south line defined by the boundary between Townships 10E and 11E, but excluding the main reservation of the Tohono O'odham Nation and excluding the Apache Junction portion of the existing Phoenix PM 10 nonattainment area. 4 77 FR 32024 (May 31, 2012). The boundaries for the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area are described in 40 CFR 81.303. As a result of the nonattainment designation, the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area was classified as a Moderate PM 10 nonattainment area with an attainment date of as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than December 31, 2018. The Arizona Department of Environmental Quality (ADEQ) submitted a SIP revision intended to meet the Moderate PM 10 nonattainment requirements on December 21, 2015 (“2015 West Pinal Plan”). On June 24, 2020, the EPA determined that West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area did not attain the 1987 PM 10 NAAQS by December 31, 2018. 5 Pursuant to CAA section 188(b)(2), the area was reclassified to “Serious” nonattainment with an attainment date of as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than December 31, 2022. 6 5 85 FR 37756 (June 24, 2020). 6 Id. On January 8, 2021, the EPA proposed to disapprove the 2015 West Pinal Plan. 7 On May 17, 2021, ADEQ withdrew the 2015 West Pinal Plan, with the exception of several rules and statutes that had been approved into the SIP in 2017. 8 Consequently, the EPA did not finalize the actions proposed on January 8, 2021, with respect to the Moderate area plan requirements. Instead, on July 23, 2021, the EPA found that Arizona had failed to submit a plan to address these requirements. 9 7 86 FR 1347 (Jan. 8, 2021). 8 Letter dated May 17, 2021, from Daniel Czecholinski, Director, Air Quality Division, ADEQ, to Deborah Jordan, Acting Regional Administrator, EPA Region IX, Subject: “RE: Withdrawal from EPA Consideration of the 2015 Arizona State Implementation Plan Revision: West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area.” 9 86 FR 38928 (July 23, 2021). On May 31, 2022, ADEQ adopted and submitted the “2022 Serious Area Particulate Plan for PM 10 for the West Pinal County Nonattainment Area” (“2022 West Pinal Plan”), 10 as a revision to the Arizona SIP. 11 In addition to addressing the Moderate and Serious area plan requirements, the 2022 West Pinal Plan included a request for an extension of the December 31, 2022 attainment date pursuant to CAA section 188(e). On November 30, 2022, the EPA issued a letter finding the 2022 West Pinal Plan complete under CAA section 110(k). 12 However, the EPA did not approve the Plan or the attainment date extension request. On May 19, 2025, ADEQ withdrew the 2022 West Pinal Plan. 13 10 West Pinal PM 10 Plan, Appendix E, Exhibit 2, Resolution to Adopt the 2022 Serious Area Particulate Plan for PM-10 for the West Pinal County Nonattainment Area. 11 Letter dated May 31, 2022, from Daniel Czecholinski, Director, Air Quality Division, ADEQ, to Martha Guzman, Regional Administrator, EPA Region IX, Subject: “Arizona State Implementation Plan Revision, Maricopa Association of Governments 2022 Serious Area Particulate Plan for PM-10 for the West Pinal County Nonattainment Area.” 12 Letter dated November 30, 2022, from Elizabeth J. Adams, Director, Air and Radiation Division, EPA Region IX, to Misael Cabrera, Director, ADEQ, Subject: “Completeness Finding for State Implementation Plan (SIP) Submission for West Pinal County for the 1987 PM 10 National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) and Termination of Clean Air Act (CAA) Sanctions Clocks.” 13 Letter dated May 15, 2025, from Daniel Czecholinkski, Director, Air Quality Division, ADEQ to Josh F.W. Cook, Regional Administrator, EPA Region IX, Subject: “Withdrawal from EPA Consideration of the 2022 Serious Area Particulate Plan for PM 10 for the West Pinal County Nonattainment Area.” On July 21, 2023, the EPA determined that the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area did not attain the 1987 PM 10 NAAQS by the December 31, 2022 Serious area attainment date. 14 Pursuant to CAA section 189(d), Arizona was required to submit a revision to the SIP for the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area by December 31, 2023. 14 88 FR 47026 (July 21, 2023). On November 29, 2023, the Maricopa Association of Governments (MAG) adopted the “2023 Five Percent Particulate Plan for PM-10 for the West Pinal County Nonattainment Area” (“2023 Five Percent Plan” or “Plan”). On December 14, 2023, ADEQ submitted the 2023 Five Percent Plan on behalf of MAG. 15 The EPA reviewed the submission for completeness under our completeness criteria in 40 CFR part 51, appendix V and determined that the submittal meets these minimum criteria on June 14, 2024. 16 The EPA is proposing approval of the submission as meeting the requirements of CAA section 189(d) as well as Moderate and Serious area requirements. 15 Letter dated December 13, 2023, from Hether Krause, Deputy Director, Air Quality Division, ADEQ to Martha Guzman, Regional Administrator, EPA Region IX, Subject: “Arizona State Implementation Plan Revision, Maricopa Association of Governments 2023 Five Percent Particulate Plan for PM-10 for the West Pinal County Nonattainment Area.” 16 Letter dated June 14, 2024, from Mathew Lakin, Director, Air and Radiation Division, EPA Region IX to Karen L. Peters, Cabinet Executive Officer, ADEQ, Subject: “Re: Completeness Finding for the State Implementation Plan (SIP) Submission for the West Pinal Nonattainment Area for the 1987 PM 10 National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS).” III. Overview of Applicable CAA Requirements As a Serious PM 10 nonattainment area that failed to attain the NAAQS by its applicable attainment date of December 31, 2022, the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area is subject to the requirements of CAA section 189(d). In addition, because the EPA has not previously approved a Moderate or a Serious area plan for the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area, the area is also required to demonstrate that it has met the requirements associated with these classifications. CAA section 189(d) provides that the State shall “submit within 12 months after the applicable attainment date, plan revisions that provide for attainment of the PM 10 air quality standard and, from the date of such submission until attainment, for an annual reduction of PM 10 or PM 10 precursor emissions within the area of not less than 5 percent of the amount of such emissions as reported in the most recent inventory prepared for the area.” The general planning and control requirements for all nonattainment plans are found in CAA sections 110 and 172. More specific planning and control requirements relevant to the PM 10 NAAQS are found in part D, subpart 4, in CAA sections 188 and 189. The EPA has issued a General Preamble 17 and Addendum to the General Preamble 18 to provide guidance to States for meeting the CAA's requirements for the PM 10 NAAQS. The General Preamble mainly addresses the requirements for Moderate nonattainment areas and the Addendum addresses the requirements for Serious nonattainment areas. The EPA has also issued other guidance documents related to PM 10 plans that are discussed and cited below. The specific PM 10 attainment planning requirements addressed by this SIP submission are summarized below. 17 “State Implementation Plans; General Preamble for the Implementation of Title I of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990,” 57 FR 13498 (Apr. 16, 1992) (“General Preamble”) and 57 FR 18070 (Apr. 28, 1992). 18 “State Implementation Plans for Serious PM-10 Nonattainment Areas, and Attainment Date Waivers for PM-10 Nonattainment Areas Generally; Addendum to the General Preamble for the Implementation of Title I of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990,” 59 FR 41998 (Aug. 16, 1994) (“Addendum”). A. Emissions Inventories CAA section 172(c)(3) requires a “base year inventory” that is a comprehensive, accurate, current inventory of actual emissions from all sources of the relevant pollutant or pollutants in the area. The plan should also include a second projected attainment year inventory for the year that the area is projected to attain the PM 10 standards. B. PM 10 Precursors CAA section 189(e) requires that the control requirements for major stationary sources of direct PM 10 also apply to major stationary sources of PM 10 precursors, except where the Administrator determines that such sources do not contribute significantly to PM 10 levels that exceed the standard in the area. While CAA section 189(e) expressly requires control of precursors from major stationary sources, subpart 4 and other CAA provisions collectively require the control of direct PM 10 and PM 10 precursors from all types of sources ( i.e., stationary sources, area sources and mobile sources) as may be needed for the purposes of demonstrating attainment as expeditiously as practicable in a given nonattainment area. 19 19 See CAA requirements for States to demonstrate attainment “as expeditiously as practicable,” CAA sections 188(c)(1) and 172(a)(1). C. Best Available Control Measures and Reasonably Available Control Measures Demonstration CAA section 189(b)(1)(B) requires that Serious area PM 10 attainment plans provide for the implementation of best available control measures (BACM) within four years of reclassification to Serious. Because the Serious area attainment date of December 31, 2022, has passed, and the EPA found that the area failed to attain by the Serious area attainment date, 20 we are evaluating the submission for compliance with the BACM requirements now, in conjunction with the State's SIP submission intended to meet the Moderate area, Serious area, and CAA section 189(d) plan requirements. Furthermore, because the EPA has not previously taken action to approve the SIP as meeting the subpart 4 reasonably available control measures (RACM) Moderate area planning requirements under CAA section 189 for the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area, the EPA is reviewing the 2023 Five Percent Plan for compliance with those requirements as well. 21 20 See note 13. 21 The EPA does not normally conduct a separate evaluation to determine whether a Serious area plan's measures also meet the RACM requirements. As explained in the Addendum to the General Preamble, we interpret the BACM requirement as generally subsuming the RACM requirement— i.e., if we determine that the measures are indeed the “best available,” we have necessarily concluded that they are “reasonably available.” (Addendum to the General Preamble, 42010). Therefore, a separate analysis to determine if the measures represent a RACM level of control is not necessary. A proposed approval of a Plan's provisions concerning implementation of BACM is also a proposed finding that the Plan provides for the implementation of RACM. D. CAA Section 189(d) Attainment Demonstration and Five Percent Requirement For Serious PM 10 nonattainment areas that do not attain the PM 10 NAAQS by the applicable attainment date, CAA section 189(d) requires the State to submit plan revisions that provide for attainment of the NAAQS ( i.e., an attainment demonstration) as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than five years from the publication date of the notice of a nonattainment finding. The plan must also provide for an annual five percent reduction in PM 10 or PM 10 precursor emissions for each year from the date of submission until attainment. CAA section 189(d) specifies that the State must submit these plan revisions within 12 months of the applicable attainment date that the area failed to meet. E. Reasonable Further Progress and Quantitative Milestones CAA section 172(c)(2) requires that implementation plans demonstrate reasonable further progress (RFP) as defined in CAA section 171(1). CAA section 171(1) defines RFP as “such annual incremental reductions in emissions of the relevant air pollutant as are required by this part [part D of title I] or may reasonably be required by the Administrator for the purpose of ensuring attainment of the applicable national ambient air quality standard by the applicable date.” The general RFP requirement of CAA section 172(c)(2) applies to SIP submissions necessary to meet CAA section 189(d) for the PM 10 NAAQS. In addition, CAA section 189(c)(1), specifically applicable to the PM 10 NAAQS, requires that an implementation plan contain quantitative milestones that will be achieved every three years and that will demonstrate that RFP is being met. F. Contingency Measures CAA section 172(c)(9) requires that implementation plans provide for “the implementation of specific measures to be undertaken if the area fails to make reasonable further progress, or to attain the NAAQS by the attainment date applicable under this part [part D of title I]. Such measures are to take effect in any such case without further action by the State or the Administrator.” The contingency measure requirement of CAA section 172(c)(9) applies to the SIP submissions necessary to meet CAA section 189(d) for the PM 10 NAAQS. G. Transportation Conformity and Motor Vehicle Emissions Budgets Transportation conformity is required by CAA section 176(c). The conformity regulations found at 40 CFR part 93, subpart A require that transportation plans, programs, and projects conform to the purpose of the SIP and establish the criteria and procedures for determining whether or not they do so. Conformity to the purpose of the SIP means that transportation activities will not produce new air quality violations, worsen existing violations, or delay timely attainment of the NAAQS or any interim milestones. Once a SIP that contains motor vehicle emissions budgets (“budgets”) has been submitted to the EPA, and the Agency has found them adequate, these budgets are used for determining conformity: emissions from planned transportation activities must be less than or equal to the budgets. 22 22 See 40 CFR 93.118(a) to (e). H. Adequate Authority CAA section 110(a)(2)(E)(i) requires that implementation plans provide necessary assurances that the State (or the general purpose local government or regional agency designated by the State for this purpose) will have adequate personnel, funding and authority under State law to carry out the requirements of such plan. Requirements for legal authority are further defined in 40 CFR part 51, subpart L (51.230-51.232) and for resources in 40 CFR 51.280. States and responsible local agencies must also demonstrate that they have the legal authority to adopt and enforce provisions of the SIP and to obtain information necessary to determine compliance. IV. Evaluation of the 2023 Five Percent Plan's Compliance With CAA Requirements A. Emissions Inventories CAA section 172(c)(3) requires all nonattainment area plans to include a base year emissions inventory that is a comprehensive, accurate, and current inventory of actual emissions from all sources of the relevant pollutant or pollutants in the area at issue. Also, the State should submit a projected attainment year emissions inventory for the year in which the State projects that the area will attain the PM 10 standards. The EPA's emission inventory guidance provides recommendations on how to develop and document emission inventories. 23 23 See “Emissions Inventory Guidance for Implementation of Ozone and Particulate Matter National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) and Regional Haze Regulations,” EPA, May 2017 (“2017 EI Guidance”). The 2023 Five Percent Plan uses a 2017 base year emissions inventory for Pinal County (“2017 PM 10 Inventory”) as a starting point in the analysis. The 2017 PM 10 Inventory was developed by ADEQ, Pinal County Air Quality Control District (PCAQCD), and MAG. The 2017 PM 10 Inventory included emissions from point sources (permitted sources), nonpoint sources (area sources), nonroad mobile sources, and on-road mobile sources. This emission inventory is sufficiently comprehensive, covering all sources of PM 10 that have been found to be important sources of relevant emissions in this and other PM 10 nonattainment areas. The 2017 PM 10 Inventory shows that the most significant sources of annual emissions in the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area are unpaved road dust: private roads (31.5 percent), unpaved road dust: agricultural roads (24.7 percent), unpaved road dust: public roads (16.2 percent), windblown dust (9.0 percent), tilling and harvesting (5.0 percent), feedlots (3.3 percent), and construction (2.7 percent). The annual and daily PM 10 emissions inventories and the emission estimation methodologies used to develop the 2017 PM 10 Inventory are described in detail in Appendix A, Exhibit 1 of the 2023 Five Percent Plan. In general, the base year emissions inventory represents the emissions contributing to the air quality problem addressed by the SIP revision. Because the EPA's final rule determining that the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area failed to attain the PM 10 standard by its attainment date used 2020-2022 monitoring data to make its determination, a year that is included within that time period and the triennial schedule of the National Emission Inventory (NEI) would generally be an appropriate base year. While the 2020 NEI year would have been the most recent such year to consider at the time of this plan's development, due to COVID-related emissions anomalies, the 2023 Five Percent Plan concludes that 2020 was not an appropriate inventory year. The base year, 2017, was chosen as it is a reasonably current NEI year, and the most recent NEI year available that was not 2020 at the time of plan development. The 2017 PM 10 Inventory includes only primary PM 10 emissions and does not include emissions for PM 10 precursors. As described in section IV.B of this document, MAG determined that precursors do not play a significant role in the PM 10 exceedances in the West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area and the EPA's analysis supports this conclusion. The 2023 Five Percent Plan includes a 2026 projected attainment year emissions inventory (“attainment year inventory”) that was developed using annual PM 10 emissions under implementation of Moderate area (existing) controls from the 2017 base year inventory through 2021 and Serious area controls from 2022 through 2026. Emission growth factors were developed for each source category relative to 2017 (growth or decline) and applied based on factors including, but not limited to, forecasted total population growth and vehicle miles traveled (VMT). Control reductions were then applied as appropriate, based on category-specific control effectiveness estimates for each individual measure. The resulting 2026 attainment year inventory was then provided for each source category and in total. 24 24 2023 Five Percent Plan, Appendix B, Exhibit I, pp. III-59-III-62. In developing the emissions inventories, MAG followed the EPA's 2017 EI Guidance and recommendations regarding the use of emission factors, activity estimates, and control factors, and the other source-specific inventory development methodologies. The relative accuracy of each estimate underwent the prescribed quality assurance procedures, documented in the State's emissions inventory preparation plan. 25 25 2023 Five Percent Plan, “Pinal County PM Inventory Preparation Plan,” Report No. SR2013-01-01, prepared by Sierra Research for the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality, February 2013. The EPA's analysis indicates the inventories are sufficiently accurate for the purposes of the 2023 Five Percent Plan. Because we find that the inventory is current, comprehensive, and accurate, we propose to approve the 2017 PM 10 base year inventory and 2026 attainment year inventory under CAA section 172(c)(3). B. PM 10 Precursors The provisions of subpart 4 of part D, title I of the CAA do not define the term “precursor” for purposes of PM 10 , nor do they explicitly require the control of any specific particulate matter (PM) precursor. The statutory definition of “air pollutant” in CAA section 302(g), however, provides that the term “includes any precursors to the formation of any air pollutant, to the extent the Administrator has identified such precursor or precursors for the particular purpose for which the term `air pollutant' is used.” The EPA has identified sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ), oxides of nitrogen (NO X ), volatile organic compounds (VOC), and ammonia (NH 3 ) as precursors to the formation of PM. 26 Accordingly, a State must include emissions of direct PM and these four precursors in emissions inventories and must control emissions from sources of all of these pollutants, unless the State demonstrates to the EPA's satisfaction that control of one or more of these pollutants is not needed for expeditious attainment of the NAAQS in the nonattainment area at issue. 26 See 81 FR 58010, 58018 (Aug. 24, 2016). title: Air Quality Plan; Arizona; Pinal County Air Quality Control District; West Pinal County PM10 Nonattainment Area; Fugitive Dust Rules
content: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY 40 CFR Part 52 [EPA-R09-OAR-2026-5581; FRL-13513-01-R9] Air Quality Plan; Arizona; Pinal County Air Quality Control District; West Pinal County PM 10 Nonattainment Area; Fugitive Dust Rules AGENCY: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). ACTION: Proposed rule. SUMMARY: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to approve revisions to the Pinal County Air Quality Control District (PCAQCD or “District”) portion of the Arizona State Implementation Plan (SIP). These revisions concern emissions of particulate matter (PM) that is 10 micrometers or smaller in diameter (PM 10 ) from fugitive dust sources, including open areas/vacant lots, unpaved lots, unpaved roads, paved public roadways, and construction sites. We are proposing to approve local rules to regulate these emission sources under the Clean Air Act (CAA or “Act”). DATES: Comments must be received on or before November 18, 2026. ADDRESSES: Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-R09-OAR-2026-5581 at https://www.regulations.gov. For comments submitted at Regulations.gov, follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Once submitted, comments cannot be edited or removed from Regulations.gov. The EPA may publish any comment received to its public docket. Do not submit electronically any information you consider to be Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. Multimedia submissions (audio, video, etc.) must be accompanied by a written comment. The written comment is considered the official comment and should include discussion of all points you wish to make. The EPA will generally not consider comments or comment contents located outside of the primary submission ( i.e., on the web, cloud, or other file sharing system). For additional submission methods, please contact the person identified in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section. For the full EPA public comment policy, information about CBI or multimedia submissions, and general guidance on making effective comments, please visit https://www.epa.gov/dockets/commenting-epa-dockets. If you need assistance in a language other than English or if you are a person with a disability who needs a reasonable accommodation at no cost to you, please contact the person identified in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section. FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Alina Batool, EPA Region IX, 75 Hawthorne St., San Francisco, CA 94105; telephone number: (415) 972-3345; email address: batool.alina@epa.gov. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Throughout this document, “we,” “us,” and “our” refer to the EPA. We use multiple abbreviations and terms in this proposed rule. While this list may not be exhaustive, for ease of reading and for reference purposes, the EPA defines the following terms and acronyms here: ADEQ—Arizona Department of Environmental Quality BACM—best available control measures CAA—Clean Air Act CBI—confidential business information CFR—Code of Federal Regulations EPA—Environmental Protection Agency IBR—incorporation by reference MSM—most stringent measures NAAQS—national ambient air quality standards PCAQCD—Pinal County Air Quality Control District PM—particulate matter PM 10 —particulate matter 10 micrometers or smaller in diameter RACT—reasonably available control technology RACM—reasonably available control measures SIP—State Implementation Plan TFV—threshold friction velocity TSD—technical support document Table of Contents I. Executive Summary A. What action is the EPA taking? B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? II. Background A. PM 10 NAAQS B. Area Description III. Summary of Arizona's Submittal A. What did Arizona submit? B. Are there other related submittals or actions? IV. The EPA's Evaluation of Arizona's Submittal A. How is the EPA evaluating the submittal? B. Does the submittal meet the evaluation criteria? C. Proposed Action and Public Comment V. Incorporation by Reference VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews I. Executive Summary A. What action is the EPA taking? The EPA is proposing to approve a February 13, 2023 SIP submittal from Arizona that includes amendments to fugitive dust rules and related test methods for the West Pinal County portion of the Arizona SIP. Table 1 lists the new or amended rules from the submittal that we are proposing to approve from the PCAQCD Code of Regulations. Table 1—PCAQCD Rules Submitted for SIP-Approval Rule section Rule title Adopted/amended Submitted Chapter 4, Article 1: West Pinal PM 10 “Serious” NAA Fugitive Dust 4-1-010 General Applicability 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 4-1-015 Exemptions 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 4-1-020 Definitions 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 4-1-030 Standards 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 4-1-040 Recordkeeping 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 4-1-045 Reporting Requirements 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 4-1-050 Records Retention 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 4-1-060 Violations 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 Chapter 4, Article 3: Construction Sites—Fugitive Dust 4-3-160 General Provisions—West Pinal PM 10 Nonattainment Area 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 4-3-170 Definitions 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 4-3-180 Dust Generating Operations—Standards, Application, Permit, Recordkeeping and Training Requirements 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 Chapter 4, Article 9: Test Methods 4-9-310 Test Methods for Stabilization for Unpaved Shoulders and Medians of Paved Roads 1/25/2023 2/13/2023 These revisions were submitted to support Arizona's attainment plan for the West Pinal County PM 10 nonattainment area, including to meet requirements for Best Available Control Measures (BACM) and Most Stringent Measures (MSM). The rules from PCAQCD, Code of Regulations, Chapter 4, Article 1, Sections 4-1-010, 4-1-015, 4-1-020, 4-1-030, 4-1-040, 4-1-045, 4-1-050, and 4-1-060, “West Pinal PM 10 Serious NAA Fugitive Dust,” (“Article 1”) regulate PM and PM 10 emissions from “non-traditional” sources of fugitive dust: open areas/vacant lots, vehicle use in open areas/vacant lots, weed abatement, unpaved lots, unpaved roads, and paved public roadways. The rules from PCAQCD, Code of Regulations Chapter 4, Article 3, Sections 4-3-160, 4-3-170, and 4-3-180 “Construction Sites—Fugitive Dust,” (“Article 3”) regulate PM and PM 10 emissions from dust generating activities performed at construction sites. Finally, the rule from PCAQCD, Code of Regulations Chapter 4, Article 9, Section 4-9-310 “Test Methods,” (“Article 9”) establishes test methods that are relied upon by Articles 1 and 3 for determining compliance with rule requirements. Additionally, we are proposing to approve the rescission of PCAQCD, Code of Regulations, Chapter 4, Article 3, Section 4-3-190, “Violations,” adopted October 28, 2015, (“Section 4-1-190”) from the SIP. If finalized as proposed, the rules listed in Table 1 of this document will be incorporated into the federally enforceable portion of the Arizona SIP and Section 4-3-190 will be removed from the Arizona SIP. B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? We are proposing this action under section 110 of the CAA. Pursuant to CAA section 110(a), States are required to submit SIPs to the EPA that provide for the implementation, maintenance, and enforcement of the national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS). CAA section 110(k) requires SIPs to meet certain procedural requirements and requires the EPA to approve or disapprove SIP submissions. CAA section 110(l) requires States to provide public notice and an opportunity for public hearing of SIP revisions prior to their submittal and prohibits the EPA from approving any SIP revisions that would interfere with attainment or maintenance of a NAAQS, reasonable further progress, or other applicable requirements of the CAA. If a SIP submittal meets all the applicable CAA requirements, then the EPA must approve the submittal under CAA section 110(k)(3). For this submittal to be approved, we must consider CAA requirements related to the emissions limitations in the submitted rules. CAA sections 110(a)(2)(A) and 302(k) require emissions limitations in the SIP to be enforceable and continuous, respectively. CAA section 172(c)(6) requires SIPs for nonattainment areas “include enforceable emissions limitations, and such other control measures means or techniques . . . as well as schedules and timetables for compliance, as may be necessary or appropriate to provide for attainment of such standard in such area by the applicable attainment date . . . .” Also, 40 CFR part 51, subpart K, requires SIPs to contain legally enforceable procedures for monitoring the status of compliance with the requirements in the control strategy. Finally, while these rules were submitted to meet BACM requirements under CAA section 189(b)(1)(B) and MSM requirements under CAA section 188(e), we are not evaluating them for BACM or MSM in this rulemaking action. We will evaluate BACM and MSM in a separate Federal Register notice in the context of the broader attainment plan action for the West Pinal County PM 10 nonattainment area. We are proposing that this submittal meets all applicable CAA requirements and are proposing to fully approve it under CAA section 110(k)(3). II. Background A. PM 10 NAAQS The EPA establishes the NAAQS for certain ambient air pollutants at levels required to protect public health and welfare. Emissions of PM 10 contribute to effects that are harmful to human health and the environment, including premature mortality, aggravation of respiratory and cardiovascular disease, decreased lung function, visibility impairment, and damage to vegetation and ecosystems. Accordingly, the EPA revised the NAAQS for particulate matter on July 1, 1987, replacing the standards for total suspended particulates, which are particles 30 micrometers or smaller in diameter, with new standards applying only to PM 10 . 1 In revising the NAAQS for particulate matter, we established a 24-hour standard of 150 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m 3 ), as well as an annual standard that was subsequently revoked in 2006. 2 1 52 FR 24634 (Jul. 1, 1987). 2 71 FR 61144 (Oct. 17, 2006). B. Area Description On May 31, 2012, the EPA designated a portion of state lands in western Pinal County, Arizona, as nonattainment for the 1987 p.m. 10 NAAQS. 3 The West Pinal County PM 10 nonattainment area encompasses approximately 1,325 square miles lying within a basin characterized by low desert valleys between the Phoenix and Tucson metropolitan areas. It includes all or portions of the incorporated cities and towns of Apache Junction, Casa Grande, Coolidge, Eloy, Florence, Queen Creek, and Maricopa, with a population of approximately 343,788 based upon July 1, 2017 U.S. Census Bureau data. Average elevation in the nonattainment area is 1,403 feet above sea level, with elevations of up to 6,441 feet directly east of the nonattainment area, which becomes more mountainous. 3 77 FR 32024 (May 31, 2012). The boundaries for the West Pinal County nonattainment area are described in 40 CFR 81.303. The West Pinal County PM 10 nonattainment area was originally classified as “Moderate” nonattainment on May 31, 2012, with an attainment date of December 31, 2018. CAA section 188(b)(2) requires the EPA to determine whether a PM 10 nonattainment area classified as Moderate has attained the 1987 24-hour PM 10 NAAQS by the area's attainment date. If the EPA determines that a Moderate area has not attained the NAAQS by the relevant attainment date, then the area shall be reclassified as a Serious area by operation of law. On June 24, 2020, we took final action to determine that the West Pinal County PM 10 nonattainment area did not attain the 1987 24-hour PM 10 NAAQS, and as a result, it was reclassified to Serious nonattainment by operation of law. 4 4 85 FR 37756 (Jun. 24, 2020). III. Summary of Arizona's Submittal A. What did Arizona submit? On February 13, 2023, the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality (ADEQ) submitted amended rules from PCAQCD to the EPA for approval into the West Pinal County portion of the Arizona SIP. The rule amendments were adopted by PCAQCD on January 25, 2023, and submitted to support Arizona's attainment plan for the West Pinal County PM 10 nonattainment area. Table 1 of this document lists the adopted and/or amended rules that were submitted and that we are proposing to approve into the SIP. The submittal also requests to rescind Section 4-3-190, which was repealed by the Pinal County Board of Supervisors on January 25, 2023. 5 Additionally, the submittal requests that we approve Section 4-3-320, “Test Methods for Stabilization for Unpaved Roads and Unpaved Parking Lots,” adopted on June 3, 2009, (“Section 4-3-320”) and 4-3-340, “Visual Opacity Test Methods,” adopted on June 3, 2009, (“Section 4-3-340”). On August 13, 2023, this submittal was deemed by operation of law to be complete. We have reviewed the submittal to ensure it meets the completeness criteria in 40 CFR part 51, appendix V. 5 Resolution No. 012523-AQ. B. Are there other related submittals or actions? We approved earlier versions of the rules in Article 1 and Article 3 into the SIP in 2017. 6 If we finalize this rulemaking as proposed, then the January 25, 2023 versions of the rules from Article 1 and Article 3, as listed in Table 1 of this document, will replace the previously approved versions in the SIP. 6 82 FR 20267 (May 1, 2017). These earlier versions were adopted by PCAQCD on October 28, 2015, and submitted to the EPA on December 21, 2015. Regarding test methods from Article 9, Section 4-9-310, “Test Methods for Stabilization for Unpaved Shoulders and Medians of Paved Roads,” adopted on January 25, 2023, (“Section 4-9-310”) has not been previously approved into the SIP. However, in 2010, we previously approved the currently submitted versions of Sections 4-9-320 and 4-9-340. 7 That is, Sections 4-9-320 and 4-9-340 are already approved into the SIP, and no further action from the EPA is needed related to the current request to approve them into the SIP. PCAQCD has not amended these rules locally. 7 75 FR 17307 (Apr. 6, 2010). Finally, PCAQCD repealed Section 4-3-190 that we previously approved into the SIP in 2017. 8 8 82 FR 20267 (May 1, 2017). IV. The EPA's Evaluation of Arizona's Submittal A. How is the EPA evaluating the submittal? Emission limitations in the SIP must be enforceable, continuous, and must not interfere with applicable requirements concerning attainment and reasonable further progress or other CAA requirements. 9 Additionally, 40 CFR part 51, subpart K, requires SIPs to have enforceable procedures for monitoring the status of compliance with the requirements in the control strategy. 9 See, CAA sections 110(a)(2), 302(k) and 110(l), respectively. The PCAQCD regulates a PM 10 nonattainment area classified as Serious for the 1987 24-hour PM 10 NAAQS. In Serious nonattainment areas, SIPs must implement BACM, including Best Available Control Technology. 10 In addition, because Arizona is seeking a five-year extension of the attainment date, the SIP must also implement MSM. 11 These evaluations are included in the context of the broader attainment plan rulemaking and are not included in this rulemaking. In this rulemaking, we are evaluating these rules for approval into the SIP under CAA section 110 requirements. 10 CAA section 189(b)(1)(B). 11 CAA section 188(e). Our evaluation also relies on relevant guidance and policy documents to evaluate enforceability and revisions/relaxation requirements. 12 12 See, “State Implementation Plans; General Preamble for the Implementation of Title I of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990,” 57 FR 13498 (Apr. 16, 1992); 57 FR 18070 (Apr. 28, 1992); “Guidance Document for Correcting Common VOC & Other Rule Deficiencies,” EPA Region 9, August 21, 2001 (the Little Bluebook); “State Implementation Plans for Serious PM-10 Nonattainment Areas, and Attainment Date Waivers for PM-10 Nonattainment Areas Generally; Addendum to the General Preamble for the Implementation of Title I of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990,” 59 FR 41998 (Aug. 16, 1994); “PM-10 Guideline Document,” EPA 452/R-93-008, April 1993; and “Fugitive Dust Background Document and Technical Information Document for Best Available Control Measures,” EPA 450/2-92-004, September 1992. B. Do the submittals meet the evaluation criteria? We evaluated these rules to ensure they meet CAA requirements and are consistent with relevant guidance regarding enforceability and SIP revisions. 1. Article 1 Rules Article 1 applies to “non-traditional” fugitive dusts sources in the West Pinal County PM 10 nonattainment area: open areas/vacant lots, vehicle use in open areas/vacant lots, unpaved lots, weed abatement and/or trash removal, unpaved roads, and paved public roadways. Affected owners and operators are required to implement control measures that will meet visible emission and surface stabilization standards. Compliance with stabilization and visible emission standards are determined through applicable test methods in Article 9. Each of the regulated activities has specific standards and control measures that must be met. For visible emission standards, either a 20 percent opacity limit applies or visible emissions, including fugitive dust, are prohibited from going beyond the property line. Owners and operators choose the stabilization standard they will meet from a list of options, such as maintaining a soil crust, meeting a minimum threshold friction velocity (TFV) 13 limit, covering the area with a certain percentage of vegetative cover, or meeting silt loading 14 limits. Owners and operators then choose a control measure to implement for each regulated activity from a menu of options, such as establishing vegetative cover, applying dust suppressants, applying water, restoring the area to an undisturbed native condition, establishing barriers to prevent unauthorized vehicle access, paving parking lots, and applying and maintaining surface gravel. Additionally, disturbed surface areas of 0.10 acres (4,356 square feet) or greater must sign up to receive the Pinal County Dust Control Forecast and ensure control measures are implemented on the day prior and day of a high dust risk forecast. 13 TFV relates to a material's susceptibility to erosion from wind. Materials with a higher TFV are less susceptible to wind erosion and are associated with lower fugitive dust emissions. 14 “Silt” refers to aggregate material (dirt, sand, rock) that has a particle size of 75 micrometers or less. “Silt loading” refers to the concentration of silt on unpaved surfaces. Higher silt loading, that is, higher concentrations of smaller particles, is associated with higher fugitive dust emissions. Article 1 includes a new standard for paving existing unpaved roadways. Beginning January 1, 2024, each city, county, or state agency with primary responsibility for any existing unpaved road within the West Pinal County PM 10 nonattainment area was required to annually pave an average of 20 percent of unpaved roads within the agency's jurisdiction. 15 Further, if the EPA determines the West Pinal County PM 10 nonattainment area failed to make reasonable further progress, or to attain the PM 10 NAAQS by the attainment date, the rules include a contingency measure where any public unpaved road with average daily trips of 26 or more will have a speed limit of 15 miles per hour. 15 Up to a maximum of 5 cumulative miles for each agency. For paved public roads, Article 1 establishes new standards by requiring street sweeping to be done by certified street sweepers and establishing paved road development standards that specify minimum surface stabilization standards for road shoulders. Each person subject to Article 1 is required to compile and retain records that provide evidence of control measure application ( i.e., receipts and/or purchase records). The records must describe the type of treatment or control measure, extent of coverage, and date applied. Records must be available to the District upon request and maintained for at least two years. Agencies subject to the road paving requirement must submit annual progress reports by January 30 of each year related to the annual road paving requirements and the number of paved roads with unpaved shoulders. Overall, the visible emission limits, stabilization standards, and control measures are tailored to minimizing fugitive dust from each type of regulated activity, result in continuous emissions limitations, and the associated recordkeeping and reporting requirements are sufficient to meet the enforceability requirements of CAA sections 110(a)(2)(A) and 172(c)(6) and 40 CFR part 51, subpart K. The amendments strengthen the existing SIP, consistent with CAA section 110(l), by expanding existing control measures, such as lowering applicability thresholds, adding or revising visible emission standards, establishing clear timelines for when control measures must be implemented, clarifying that control measures are considered to be implemented when the associated visible emission and/or stabilization standards are met, and adding new control measures for paved and unpaved roads. Because they meet all applicable CAA requirements, we propose approving the rules from Article 1 into the Arizona SIP. 2. Article 3 Rules Article 3 applies to fugitive dusts sources at construction sites within the West Pinal County PM 10 nonattainment area. Affected owners and operators are required to implement control measures and meet visible emission standards and surface stabilization standards for dust generating activities. Additionally, owners or operators are required to obtain a dust permit when dust-generating operations at construction sites disturb a total surface area of 0.10 acres (4,356 square feet) or more. All permit applications must contain a dust control plan that identifies all control measures to be implemented before, after, and while conducting any dust-generating operation. Sites with a dust control permit must: for each project of 5 or more acres, have a project information sign that identifies how the public can file a dust complaint to the District; meet dust control training requirements once every three years from the District; except in certain high wind conditions, implement all control measures necessary to maintain soil stability; implement control measures specified for each type of activity, such as active areas, demolition, weed abatement, trackout, site grade preparation, trenching, and haul roads; limit dust generated on the property to 20 percent opacity, and ensure no visible emissions, including fugitive dust, go beyond the property line; install no trespassing signs for project sites when activities cease for 30 or more days at a time; and, on a high dust risk day, continue to implement control measures that maintain compliance with the applicable standards or cease dust-generating activities and ensure disturbed surface areas are stablized for the day. Construction sites that do not require a dust control permit are subject to the same general control measures, visible emission standards, and stabilization requirements but are not subject to signage and dust control training requirements. Similar to Article 1, owners and operators subject to Article 3 choose from a menu of options to meet control measure requirements and surface stabilization standards. Any person who conducts dust-generating operations that require a dust control permit is required to keep written records of self-inspection on each day dust-generating operations are conducted. Self-inspection records include daily inspections for crusted or damp soil, trackout conditions and clean-up measures, daily water usage for dust control measures, and dust suppressant application. Any person who conducts dust-generating operations that do not require a dust control permit must maintain records that provide evidence of control measure application, by indicating the type of treatment or control measure, extent of coverage, and date applied. Records are required to be maintained for two years, except for construction sites at a facility with a title V operating permit, which must maintain records for five years. Overall, the dust control permit requirements, visible emission limits, stabilization standards, and control measures are tailored to minimizing fugitive dust for each type of regulated activity, result in continuous emission limitations, and associated recordkeeping requirements are sufficient to meet the enforceability requirements of CAA sections 110(a)(2)(A) and 172(c)(6) and 40 CFR part 51, subpart K. The amendments would strengthen the existing SIP in several ways, consistent with CAA section 110(l), including adding a visible emission standard that prohibits visible emissions from going beyond the property line, adding signage requirements and dust control operator training requirements, specifying the threshold for obtaining a dust control permit, specifying the dust generating activities that are required to implement control measures, specifying the types of control measures that apply to each type of dust generating activity, specifying that control measures must be implemented at all times, and requiring daily records of actions to reduce fugitive dust. Because they meet all applicable CAA requirements, we are proposing to approve the rules from Article 3 into the Arizona SIP. 3. Rescission of Section 4-3-190 Previously, if certain conditions were met, Section 4-3-190 provided an exemption from the requirements of Article 3 during high wind conditions and emergency maintenance of flood control channels and water retention basins. The rule amendments adopted by the District to Article 3 on January 25, 2023, incorporate requirements that apply during these circumstances within other provisions of Article 3 such that removal of this section would not relax any existing SIP requirement and is consistent with CAA section 110(l). 16 Therefore, we are proposing to approve this rescission request. 16 See, Section 4-3-180.I.2.b, contains required control measures during high wind events, Section 4-3-170.20, adds a definition for “high wind conditions,” and Section 4-3-160.A.5.i is a comparable exemption for emergency maintenance of flood control channels, conditioned on implementation of all permitted control measures. 4. Article 9 Rules Section 4-9-310 establishes test methods to determine whether unpaved shoulders and medians of paved roads meet applicable surface stabilization standards. It includes an opacity test method, silt loading test method, and gravel depth and silt content test method. These test methods are used to determine compliance with stabilization standards in Article 1 and 3. Based upon our evaluation, these test methods are enforceable and consistent with comparable test methods established in Federal requirements and SIP-approved fugitive dust rules in other States. We consider their use with Articles 1 and 3 to be an appropriate application of the test methods. The test methods ensure the associated emission limits will meet the enforceability requirements of CAA sections 110(a)(2)(A) and 172(c)(6) and 40 CFR part 51, subpart K, strengthen the SIP, and would not interfere with any other CAA requirements, consistent with CAA section 110(l). Because the rule meets all applicable CAA requirements, we are proposing to approve Section 4-9-310 into the Arizona SIP. As stated above in section III.B, the EPA is not acting on Sections 4-9-320 and 4-9-340 from the state's submittal in this action. These rules are already approved into the SIP and PCAQCD has not amended them locally, so no further action is needed. 5. Conclusions Based on our review, the rules proposed for approval, as listed in Table 1 of this document, and the proposed rescission of Section 4-3-190 meet the relevant CAA requirements. The technical support documents (TSDs) for each article (Articles 1, 3, and 9) have more information on our evaluation and are available in the docket for this rulemaking. C. Proposed Action and Public Comment As authorized in section 110(k)(3) of the Act, the EPA proposes to approve Arizona's February 13, 2023 SIP submittal, including approving the rules listed in Table 1 of this document into the Pinal County portion of the Arizona SIP and the rescission of Section 4-3-190 from the SIP, because they fulfill all relevant requirements. We will accept comments from the public on this proposal until November 18, 2026. If finalized as proposed, our final action will incorporate the rules listed in Table 1 of this document into the federally enforceable SIP and Section 4-3-190 will be removed from the SIP. V. Incorporation by Reference In this document, the EPA is proposing to include in a final EPA rule regulatory text that includes incorporation by reference. In accordance with requirements of 1 CFR 51.5, the EPA is proposing to incorporate by reference PCAQD, Code of Regulations, Chapter 4, Article 1, Sections 4-1-010, “General Applicability;” 4-1-015, “Exemptions;” 4-1-020, “Definitions;” 4-1-030, “Standards;” 4-1-040, “Recordkeeping;” 4-1-045, “Reporting Requirements;” 4-1-050, “Records Retention;” and 4-1-060, “Violations;” as amended on January 25, 2023, which regulate fugitive dust emissions from open areas/vacant lots, unpaved lots, weed abatement, unpaved roads, and paved public roadways in the West Pinal County Serious PM 10 Nonattainment Area. The EPA is also proposing to incorporate by reference PCAQD, Code of Regulations, Chapter 4, Article 3, Sections 4-3-160, “General Provisions—West Pinal PM 10 Nonattainment Area;” 4-3-170, “Definitions;” and 4-3-180 “Dust Generating Operations: Standards, Application, Permit, Recordkeeping and Training Requirements” as amended on January 25, 2023, which regulate fugitive dust emissions from construction sites in the West Pinal County Serious PM 10 Non
